feedback: If a learner predicts the shiny foil will be slippery and is surprised, name the lesson: shiny but rough still grips — shininess was a distraction.
Keep the variable clean: compare smoothness vs roughness, and do not compare a rolling object with a sliding one as if they were the same.
If asked about tray vs glass, steer toward the surfaces in contact (how rough/smooth they are and what they are made of), not how they look; testing is the way to find out.
activities.intendedInsight: Shininess does not determine friction; what matters is the surfaces in contact: mainly how rough or smooth they are, and also what they are made of. 'Shiny = slippery' is a trap.
learnerActions: Take two surfaces: crumpled-then-flattened kitchen foil (shiny but rough) and a sheet of matte-smooth card (dull but smooth).
Predict which lets the same block slide further, and say WHY before testing.
Slide the block on each with the same push and observe which surface lets it slide further; in most setups the block grips the crinkled shiny foil more and slides further on the smooth dull card.
Explain what your results suggest mattered (usually roughness, not shininess) and restate that friction is a force from the surfaces opposing motion.
Extra challenge: would a coin slide the same on a shiny metal tray and a shiny sheet of glass? Discuss what really decides it.
activities.title: Shiny is not the same as slippery (predict–observe–explain)

feedback: Full response: 'The block stops sooner on the rough carpet; the rough surface produces more friction — a force between block and surface acting against its motion; the smooth table has less friction so it slides further.'

If a learner says the block stopped because 'the push ran out' with no mention of the surface, re-run the same push on two surfaces so the only difference is the surface, forcing them to attribute the different distance to friction (reteach pushes-as-forces if the link is missing).
If a learner only says 'rough = slow, smooth = fast' as a surface property, push for the force language: the surfaces rubbing push back against the motion.

If a learner claims a pushed-but-still block has no friction, introduce grip (static): with nothing pushing there is no horizontal friction, but a shoe or block will not slide until pushed hard — static friction is balancing the push before movement.

Watch for backwards reasoning: 'it took a long time to stop, so friction was small' only holds if the test was fair (same object, same push, only the surface changed); otherwise ask what else could have changed, such as the push or the object.
activities.intendedInsight: A full understanding names friction as a FORCE between the two surfaces, acting opposite the motion and larger on rough surfaces, predicts the stopping order for a new pair of surfaces, and recognises that friction can also act on a still object being pushed or on a slope (grip/static friction balancing the push).
learnerActions: Order a set of surfaces by how far the object slides on each (furthest → stops soonest).
Sort everyday situations into friction that is helpful (walking, braking) versus unhelpful (slowing a sledge).
Match each surface to a grip or slip description.

Answer the diagnostic: 'I slide the same wooden block across a smooth table and across a rough carpet, giving the same push each time. On which surface does it stop sooner — and what about that surface stops it?' Give the mechanism, not just the outcome.
Reason about a still object: if you push gently on a block resting on a table but it does not move, is any friction acting on it? How could you tell (what happens as you push harder)?
activities.title: Consolidate and check: sort, order, and explain
